newsitem.title: USA: Storm hammers U.S. Northwest, causes flooding.
newsitem.headline: Storm hammers U.S. Northwest, causes flooding.

text.p: A powerful New Year's Day storm hammered the U.S. Northwest on Wednesday, causing mudslides and power outages in Washington state and flooding in northern California's wine country.
The latest in a series of punishing Pacific storms that have pounded the region since last week brought heavy rain and high winds, putting a damper on New Year's celebrations.
Washington Gov. Mike Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 19 counties hit by the storms that have flooded homes and businesses and caused havoc on the roads.
At least 11 deaths are blamed on the storms and property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California is estimated at up to $250 million.

Torrential rain fell over northern California and the National Weather Service predicted "disastrous" flood levels for the flood-prone Russian and Napa rivers in the wine country north of San Francisco.
Record flooding is possible on both rivers, according to National Weather Service meteorologist Dan Weygand.

The Russian River was expected to rise to nearly 49 feet (14.8 metres) in the town of Guerneville by Wednesday evening, 17 feet (5.1 metres) above flood stage, and the Napa River was predicted to crest 6 feet (1.8 metres) above flood stage at St. Helena.

Between 4 and 6 inches (10 and 15 cms) of rain had fallen in the last 24 hours north of San Francisco and about the same amount again was forecast for the next 24 hours, Weygand said. Homes, businesses and roads in low-lying areas near the Russian River were already flooded and local officials were urging residents to leave.
"The picture is not looking good today at all," said Janice Atkinson, a spokeswoman for the Sonoma County Office of Emergency Services, which monitors the Russian River.
"Roads in the area are going under water faster than we can keep a list of them. Residents are urged to evacuate as soon as possible," she said.
Fifty-nine people spent Tuesday night at a Red Cross shelter in nearby Sebastopol but that number was expected to "increase dramatically throughout the day," she said.

In Washington state, high winds knocked down trees and power lines, leaving more than 100,000 customers in nine counties around Seattle without electricity on Wednesday, Betty Werblun, a spokeswoman for Puget Sound Power and Light Co. said.
In Snohomish County northeast of Seattle, a search and rescue team was looking for three hikers who were due back last Sunday from a snowshoeing trip in the mountains but had not yet returned.

The bad weather caused countless road closures, mudslides and sinkholes. Twenty-six homes had to be evacuated when a huge sinkhole opened in a street in Shoreline, a suburb north of Seattle. A mudslide knocked at least one home off its foundation in the wealthy Seattle neighbourhood of Magnolia.

"We still have flood warnings in effect for 17 rivers both in eastern and western Washington and some of those are expected to crest this evening," Denise Clifford, a spokeswoman for Washington Emergency Management, said.

About 400 people spent Tuesday night in 16 shelters throughout the state and another 50 homes were evacuated because of flooding in the town of Pomeroy in southeastern Washington state, Clifford said.

Several containers of hazardous material fell off a Burlington Northern Santa Fe freight train on Wednesday after three cars derailed near the town of Snohomish, about 35 miles (55 km) north of Seattle, but there were no spills, a county official said.
